### Idea

In the trail-running podcast The Albon Way, I heard John Albon describe training as a card-based system. It immediately clicked with me.

I could vividly picture the idea of running training cards, and I wanted to turn that picture into something real. The concept was to create a set of training cards, a bit like Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh, or Cars cards, but built specifically for running. Each card would capture something practical about a training element, such as what exactly to do, its strengths, what it does, when to use it, and who it is for.

Those cards would not just be loose notes. I had a very clear picture of how they could look and work, and that visual idea appealed to me a lot. I wanted them to follow a clear underlying structure while still appearing as real cards in a clean and intuitive user experience. In my head, it was something that could live inside an application and feel easy to browse, almost like a small training deck you could choose from naturally.

The reason this idea appealed to me is that training decisions can be mentally tiring. I usually know roughly where I am in a training period, but after a full day of work I do not always want to think too much about what the next session should be. I wanted this to become a quick tool that would reduce decision fatigue, make daily training choices easier, and give me a few ready-made options to choose from. At the same time, it would educate me about training along the way and make it easier for both newer and more experienced athletes to think about training, effort, and purpose in a clearer way.

The goal was also not to write all of the training content by myself. Instead, I wanted to use an AI agent as a kind of specialized coach, guided by prompts and grounded in publications, training principles, and established endurance knowledge, to help prepare and structure the cards. That way, the training logic would come from a more expert-like source, while I focused on the infrastructure and the overall system.

In a way, the project became a mix of my own ideas, AI support, and careful supervision. A lot of the implementation came together with AI support, but the structure, the card system, and the direction were still strongly shaped by my input. I also wanted the whole thing to stay easy to maintain, adjust, and reuse over time, so the cards would not just live inside this repo, but could also be reused in other projects that would bring the to life. This repo holds the card content and outputs it in a structured, way using a class-based setup.

### Training Cards Structure

The training-card schema is buit and organized as a ssmall vocabulary for coaching. The training plan has layers, so, the card's structure follows a simple hierarchy that mirrors the way the content is meant to be understood. At the top level, the model uses a few controlled types and a shared base class, then extends that base with more specialized card types. That gives the library one consistent structure while still letting each level carry the information it needs.

The basic idea is simple: a training plan is made of layers, and each layer has a different job. The card system mirrors that coaching reality.

- *macro* block is the big phase of training and answers "What is the long-term direction?"
    - *mezzo* block is the focused block and answers: "What block are we building inside that phase?"
        - *micro* block is the week that shapes the load and answers: "What does this week need to do?"
            - *session* is the workout itself and answers: "What workout should we do today?"


Those are different planning levels and the usuall training usualy reflects that hierarchy. 

#### Shared Base Class

`BaseTrainingCard` is the shared foundation for all card types. It creates the stable frame that every specialized card can build on and is the core definition of what a card is. It holds the fields every card needs to be identified, understood, displayed, and connected to other cards. 

It answers questions like:
- What fields does a training card have?
- What does each field mean?
- What shape is valid for a card?

So it separates:

- What must always be there
- What is useful but not always present
- What only belongs to a specific card level

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class BaseTrainingCard:
    id: str
    slug: str
    title: str
    card_type: CardType
    suitable_levels: list[TrainingLevel]
    summary: str
    purpose: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    goal_race_context: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    training_profile: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    expected_adaptations: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    watchouts: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    progression_rules: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    regression_rules: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    additional_information: str = ""
    references: list[CardReference] = field(default_factory=list)
```

Each card object has a fixed set of allowerd fields (`slots=True`). The identity and core coaching fields - `id`, `slug`, `title`, `card_type`, `suitable_levels`, `summary` and `purpose` are required because they have no default value in the schema. The remaining fields are optional because they add detail without being necessary to identify the card. This keeps the schema balanced: strict enough to trust and support coaching, but not so strict that writing cards becomes frustrating.

For the class fields, we used `str` when a field should hold one clear coaching idea and `list[str]` when it should hold several short coaching points. `default_factory` helps avoid shared mutable defaults.

The explanation of some fields is as follows:
- `id` is a unique identifier for the card. It is the internal name the system uses to tell cards apart.
- `slug`: a readable identifier for URLs, filenames, or search. Short, clear, and easy to recognize at a glance.
- `title`: the coach-facing name of the card. The label a coach would naturally use when talking about the card.
- `tags`: quick labels for search or grouping. Help identify related cards quickly without needing to read the full content.
- `references`: links to related cards. Connect the card to its parent, child, companion, or support cards.

#### Specialized Card Classes

`MacroCard` represents the highest planning granularity over several weeks or more. It should help answer: what are we trying to accomplish over the next few weeks, and why is this the right time for it?

It inherits the shared contract (`class MacroCard(BaseTrainingCard)`) and adds the fields that matter only for a broad phase-level object.

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MacroCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_weeks: str = ""
    timing_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

`MezzoCard` is the intermediate block layer. It answers: what are we sharpening inside this phase, and how should this block sit between the macro plan and the weekly load? It is specific enough to matter, but still broad enough to support several weeks of planning without over-prescribing every day.

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MezzoCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_weeks: str = ""
    placement_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

`MicroCard` is the week-level planning card. It is the bridge between the block-level intention and the day-by-day reality of training. It describes how a coach shapes one training week to support the larger block.

```python
class MicroCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_days: str = ""
    week_structure: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    key_sessions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    load_pattern: str = ""
    placement_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    recovery_requirements: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

`SessionCard` is the most detailed card. It describes one workout or session pattern. It needs enough structure to guide execution, but it should still feel like a reusable workout concept rather than a one-off prescription. It should say not just what the workout is, but how to coach it well and what to watch for while it is happening.

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class SessionCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    session_family: str = ""
    typical_duration: str = ""
    workout_parts: list[SessionPart] = field(default_factory=list)
```

`SessionPart` is the internal building block inside a session card. Its fields should read like a workout prescription. It breaks a workout into the same language used in daily practice.

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class SessionPart:
    name: str
    duration: str
    rpe: str
    instructions: str = ""
    terrain_notes: str = ""
```

#### Supporting Classes

To keep the schema compact and consistent, the card classes are supported by a few small helper types.

`CardType` defines the four main card labels: *macro*, *mezzo*, *micro*, and *session*. Using an *enum* here keeps the hierarchy explicit and avoids scattering free-text type names throughout the code. It also makes the model easier to validate, compare, and extend later.

```python
class CardType(StrEnum):
    MACRO = "macro"
    MEZZO = "mezzo"
    MICRO = "micro"
    SESSION = "session"
```

`TrainingLevel` is another controlled vocabulary. It describes who a card is suitable for, using a small fixed set of levels instead of arbitrary strings. That keeps the schema readable and prevents the same concept from being written in slightly different ways across different cards.

```python
class TrainingLevel(StrEnum):
    ALL = "all"
    BEGINNER = "beginner"
    INTERMEDIATE = "intermediate"
    ADVANCED = "advanced"
    ELITE = "elite"
```

`CardRelationship` describes how one card connects to another. A card can point to a *parent*, *child*, *previous*, *next*, *alternative*, or *support* card. That makes the relationships part of the model itself, rather than something hidden in descriptive text.

```python
class CardRelationship(StrEnum):
    PARENT = "parent"
    CHILD = "child"
    PREVIOUS = "previous"
    NEXT = "next"
    ALTERNATIVE = "alternative"
    SUPPORT = "support"
```

`CardReference` is the small object that ties those pieces together. It stores the target card id, the relationship type, and a small list of optional tags. So instead of using loose links, the schema keeps references structured and machine-readable. That makes the library easier to navigate, easier to reuse, and easier to keep consistent as it grows.

Each card can carry structured references to other cards. That makes the relationships explicit, machine-readable, and easy to reuse later. For this we have a `CardReference` class that captures the relationship between cards and allows for small tags to add context.

A reference can say whether another card is a parent, child, previous card, next card, or simply related in some useful way. It also allows small tags to add context without turning the main card into a cluttered object. In practice, this means the structure is not just a flat list of cards. It is a connected library where relationships are part of the data model itself.

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class CardReference:
    card_id: str
    relationship: CardRelationship
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```
